title: The Handshake Loan: Why Family and Friends Funding Needs a Paper Trail Before It Becomes a Problem
excerpt: Money borrowed from family or friends rarely gets formal paperwork at the time. It becomes a real problem later, when a bank, investor or buyer asks what that money actually is.
content:
Most capital conversations start with banks, investors or a line of credit. For a meaningful number of East Coast SMEs, though, the first money into the business came from somewhere far less formal: a parent's deposit, a sibling's fifty thousand dollars, a friend who backed the idea before anyone else would. Writing it up properly feels almost rude in the moment. Family trusts family, and a loan agreement can feel like it puts a wall between two people who don't need one.

The absence of paperwork rarely causes a problem in year one. It becomes a problem the day the business approaches a bank for a facility, brings in an investor properly, or receives a genuine offer to buy. That's when someone outside the family, a credit team, a due diligence accountant, a buyer's lawyer, asks the one question an informal arrangement was never built to answer: is this money a loan, a gift, or a stake in the business?

Why an Undocumented Loan Reads as a Red Flag to Everyone Else

A lender assessing a facility needs a clean picture of every existing claim on the business before deciding how much more it can safely carry. An informal arrangement with a family member sits awkwardly in that picture. If it's treated as a liability, it reduces the capacity a new lender will extend. If it's unclear whether it's even a liability, the lender simply pauses the file until someone resolves the ambiguity. The pattern we typically see across owner-led businesses is a parent or sibling with money genuinely in the business, with no document anywhere confirming what that money actually is. Working through that properly, well before a lender or investor conversation, is exactly what a capital raise preparation process is designed to surface early rather than mid-negotiation.

The Difference Between a Gift, a Loan and a Stake

These three things are treated completely differently once someone outside the family looks at them, and informal arrangements tend to drift between all three depending on who you ask. A gift carries no expectation of repayment and generally sits outside the business's liabilities. A loan carries a genuine expectation of repayment, which means it belongs on the balance sheet and directly affects how a bank reads serviceability on top of it. A stake means the person who put money in actually owns part of the business, which has to be reflected in the ownership register and in any future valuation conversation. The owner usually has a clear view of which of the three it was meant to be. The family member's understanding, several years and one difficult trading period later, does not always match.

What a Clean Paper Trail Actually Takes

None of this requires a forty page facility agreement. It needs a one page loan agreement setting out the principal, the term, an interest rate (even a modest one) and the repayment schedule, recorded the same way every year rather than quietly renegotiated depending on how trading went. A bookkeeper or BAS agent will record a loan exactly as instructed, which is precisely their role and one they handle well. The decision about whether the money is debt or equity, and the discipline of documenting it that way from the first dollar, sits above that, in the commercial layer a bookkeeper isn't engaged to manage.

Fixing It Before a Raise or a Sale Forces the Issue

The cleanest time to sort this out is months before anyone outside the family needs an answer, not in the middle of a term sheet negotiation or a buyer's due diligence request. A Capital Raise Feasibility assessment is a useful forcing function for this, because it asks the question directly as part of working out what the business can actually raise and from whom, rather than leaving it to surface later under time pressure.

Getting a handshake loan onto paper is a half day conversation when there's no deadline attached to it. Left until a lender or a buyer asks the question directly, it becomes a far longer one, run on someone else's timeline and someone else's terms. If informal funding is sitting somewhere in the business and a growth decision or ownership conversation is approaching, a fractional CFO is well placed to get it structured properly before it needs defending. For an outside read on where things currently stand, booking a discovery call is usually the simplest first step.

faqs.q: Does a loan from a family member need a formal agreement in Australia?
faqs.a: It isn't a legal requirement in the way a bank loan is, but it becomes important the moment anyone outside the family looks closely at the business, a lender, an investor or a buyer. A simple written agreement covering the amount, term and repayment basis removes the ambiguity that causes delays later. A capital raise preparation review is a good prompt to get this sorted properly.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a loan from a relative and a gift into the business?
faqs.a: A gift carries no expectation of repayment and generally doesn't sit on the business's books as a liability. A loan does carry that expectation, which means it affects how much additional debt a bank will consider the business able to service. The distinction needs to be clear and consistent from the start, not decided retrospectively once someone asks.

faqs.q: Why do banks ask about informal loans from family when assessing a business for finance?
faqs.a: A bank needs an accurate picture of every existing claim on the business before extending new credit. An undocumented arrangement makes that picture unclear, which slows the assessment or reduces what the bank is willing to lend. A fractional CFO can help get the full liability picture clean before that conversation starts.

faqs.q: Can an undocumented family loan affect a business sale or valuation?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer's due diligence process will ask what every amount on the balance sheet, and sometimes off it, actually represents. An informal family loan without clear terms raises questions about whether it's debt to be repaid or a claim on ownership, which can stall negotiations. Resolving it is part of genuine exit readiness, ideally long before a buyer is in the picture.

faqs.q: Does my bookkeeper need to record a loan from a family member?
faqs.a: Yes, once the terms are decided, a bookkeeper or BAS agent will record the loan correctly in the accounts, which is exactly the role they play well. The earlier decision, whether the money is genuinely a loan, a gift or a stake, sits above bookkeeping, in the commercial structuring conversation that needs to happen first.

faqs.q: How much interest should a family loan into a business carry?
faqs.a: There's no single figure that applies to every business, but the arrangement should reflect a genuine, modest commercial rate rather than zero, and that rate should be fixed in writing rather than revisited informally each year. Consistency matters more to a future lender or buyer than the exact number chosen.

faqs.q: What does a capital raise feasibility assessment cover?
faqs.a: It looks at whether the business is ready to raise debt, mezzanine or equity, which instrument genuinely fits, and what realistic terms a lender or investor would offer today. Existing informal funding, including money from family or friends, is exactly the kind of detail this process is designed to surface and resolve. The Capital Raise Feasibility engagement is built around this question.
